messages.subject: Re: Labels on stacked bar plot with facet_wrap
messages.subject_clean: Labels on stacked bar plot with facet_wrap
messages.body_plain:
This gets pretty close, but it ain't pretty due to the smaller values. You could shrink the size of the font in geom_text, but that will only get you so far before it's not readable.

require(ggplot2)
require(scales)
require(RColorBrewer)
require(plyr)
require(reshape2)

m.ex<-melt(ddply(example, .(GroupingVar, FacetVar), function(x) table(x$VarOfInterest)))

m.ex2<-ddply(m.ex, .(GroupingVar,FacetVar), transform, pct=value/sum(value))

m.ex2<-ddply(m.ex2, .(GroupingVar,FacetVar), transform, half=pct/2)

m.ex2<-ddply(m.ex2, .(GroupingVar,FacetVar), transform, cum=cumsum(pct))

m.ex2<-ddply(m.ex2, .(GroupingVar,FacetVar), transform, position=(cum-half))

ggplot() + geom_bar(data=example,aes(x=GroupingVar, fill=VarOfInterest), position='fill') +

scale_fill_manual(values = (brewer.pal(5, "Greens"))) +

geom_text(data=m.ex2, aes(y=position, x=GroupingVar, label=round(pct, digits=2)))+
facet_wrap(~FacetVar,ncol=1) +
coord_flip()+
scale_y_continuous(labels=percent) + ylab('Percentage')

messages.subject: plotmatrix question
messages.subject_clean: plotmatrix question
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have two questions regarding the plotmatrix() function.

First, I have many variables and want to use plotmatrix to see their correlations. The scales of these variables are quite different, some are from 0 to 1, and some are from 0 to 1000. It seems that y axis of all matrix has a uniform scale and is really large to capture the one with biggest y value. The ones with small range are squeezed and cannot be clearly seen. I wonder is there option to fix this.

My second question is that is there a way to show the correlation coefficient on such a plot. Thanks for your input in advance!

Xiaoyu

messages.subject: Re: changing sequence of default colors
messages.subject_clean: changing sequence of default colors
messages.body_plain:
If your colors are based on factor variables, you can always rearrange
them (?levels) into the 'correct' order. In addition, I'd suggest
reading ?scale_colour_brewer and associated pages. These give lots of
examples of using a particular palette.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Xiaoyu,

Have you looked at ggpairs from the GGally package, which is a plot matrix extension for ggplot2?

I read somewhere before that somebody recommended use ggpairs instead of plotmatrix, because ggpairs provides a vastly improved pairs plot.

http://rgm2.lab.nig.ac.jp/RGM2/func.php?rd_id=GGally%3aggpairs

On the other hand, I am still interested to learn how you managed the scales with plotmatrix using scale package…I appreciate if you could post some example.

Thank you,

Kaori

messages.subject: Re: changing sequence of default colors
messages.subject_clean: changing sequence of default colors
messages.body_plain:
Hi SP

A factor can have many levels even if they don't appear in a given data frame.  So as you as your factor in each data.frame has all four levels defined and they are in the same order, they will always be coloured similarly.

That's my understanding at least.

So if you have two levels, Apple and Orange, but other levels are possible (in other datasets) like Banana and Pear, then you can define:

factor(c("Apple", "Apple", "Orange"), levels = c("Apple", "Orange", "Banana", "Pear"))

The unused levels will still be "assigned" colours (according to the order they in which they appear in your levels definition).

Regards,
Benjamin

messages.subject: Retaining all the levels of a factor in a legend (even unused ones)
messages.subject_clean: Retaining all the levels of a factor in a legend (even unused ones)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Does anyone know how I can retain all the levels of a factor in the legend even if they don't appear on the plot? I'm creating two plots of subsets of the same dataset. It just happens that the factor I'm using to colour the plot shapes is bisected into two groups by the subsetting. I want to be able to create a single legend spanning both plots which contains all the values (not just those in one subset). The problem currently is that plots reuse the same colours for different levels (and unused factor levels disappear).

I've tried to use the mtcars data set to make a little example showing what I mean:

data(mtcars)
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)

# Turn some of data into factors
mtcars$gear <- factor(mtcars$gear)
mtcars$carb <- factor(mtcars$carb)

# Create two subsets of data with divergent properties
data.a <- mtcars[mtcars$gear %in% c("4","5") & mtcars$carb %in% c("1","2"), ]
data.b <- mtcars[mtcars$gear %in% c("1","2","3") & !mtcars$carb %in% c("1","2"), ]

# All the levels still appear in the subsets (e.g. I've not used droplevels())
levels(data.a$carb)
levels(data.b$carb)

plot.a <- ggplot(data.a, aes(cyl, mpg)) + geom_point(aes(colour = carb)) + theme_bw() + theme(legend.position="top")
plot.b <- ggplot(data.b, aes(cyl, mpg)) + geom_point(aes(colour = carb)) + theme_bw() + theme(legend.position="top")
grid.arrange(plot.a, plot.b, ncol=2)

What you should see are two side-by-side plots with the legends at the top. Both will contain a pink and blue key entry, however, these colours will not refer to the same carb values.

Thanks,
Alastair

messages.subject: specifying both brow and ncol in facet_wrap
messages.subject_clean: specifying both brow and ncol in facet_wrap
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

In earlier versions of ggplot2 it was possible to specify both ncol and nrow in facet_wrap at the same time. If the number of faceting levels were lower than ncol*nrow the resulting plot would just leave the rest of the plotting areas empty. This was useful for multipage plots where the last page might contain less panels than the rest but maintain the size of the individual panels.

This behavior has changed so that now ggplot2 forces one of either ncol or brow down to a value where the plotarea is almost filled out.

For instance the following

data <- data.frame(a=1:10, b=1:10, c=rep(c('a','b','c','d','e'), each=2))
qplot(data=data, x=a, y=b, geom='point') + facet_wrap(~c, ncol=4, nrow=5, shrink=F)

creates a panel layout equivalent to ncol=4, nrow=2 instead of the one specified.

Is this change intentional and if so is it possible to have a switch to in facet_wrap to avoid it?

best wishes

Thomas

messages.subject: Re: Unwanted horizontal white lines on a ggplot map
messages.subject_clean: Unwanted horizontal white lines on a ggplot map
messages.body_plain:
It's poor form to answer your own question, but I found the answer and it might help someone else.

ggplot seems sensitive to irregularly spaced lat/lon matrix. The following code will cause horizontal white lines on my system:

Lat <- seq(0, 1, length.out=640)
Lon <- seq(0, 1, length.out=640)

Lat[50]=Lat[50]+0.00001

LatLong <- expand.grid(lat=Lat, lon=Lon)
PlotData <- data.frame(LatLong, fill=rep("#000000", 640*640))

Plot <- ggplot()
Plot <- Plot + geom_raster(aes(x = lon, y = lat, fill = fill), data = PlotData)
print(Plot)

However, removing that third line eliminates the problem.

My Lat/Lon coordinates were generated by XY2LatLon from the RgoogleMaps library. Once I have them in hand I clean them up a bit with:

Latitudes <- seq(range(Latitudes)[1], range(Latitudes)[2], length.out=length(Latitudes))
Longitudes <- seq(range(Longitudes)[1], range(Longitudes)[2], length.out=length(Longitudes))

That causes the spacing to be more even, and it eliminates those white lines in my output.

Ed

messages.subject: Re: math symbols facet_wrap (facet labels)
messages.subject_clean: math symbols facet_wrap (facet labels)
messages.body_plain:
To get math expressions in facet_grid labels, you can use
labeller=label_parsed:

m <- mpg
levels(m$drv) <- c("x[1]", "y^2", "z+3")

ggplot(m, aes(x = displ, y = cty)) + geom_point() +
    facet_grid(. ~ drv, labeller = label_parsed)

But this doesn't work with facet_wrap -- it's kind of complicated, but
the root reason it doesn't work has to do with the way the facets are
generated when you have two faceting variables. Notice the difference
between these two:

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = cty)) + geom_point() +
  facet_grid(. ~ drv + fl)

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = cty)) + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap( ~ drv + fl)

More information on why it won't work here:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/pull/656

-Winston

you have the latest version of devtools, you can do this:
  install_github('ggplot2', pull=656, ref=NULL)

and put the pieces back together in another gtable.

These recent discussions might give you an idea of how that would be done:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/ggplot2/ig5hM0F6ewc/o89T8U2SPzQJ
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/ggplot2/TCRmlKRF4ys/5j1IC7LpIsoJ

Both of these options are hacks. They're good for getting it done now,
but not for the long run.

-Winston

messages.subject: adding title and excluding objects using gtable
messages.subject_clean: adding title and excluding objects using gtable
messages.body_plain:
Following is a code example to create two plots with common legend. My questions are:
1. Is it possible to exclude the title & legend from gt1 using gtable_filter?
2. Is there a better or easy way to add just a global title without extracting the ttitle from a plot?

Thanks,
Herbert
---------------
df.d <- data.frame(x=rnorm(100), y=rnorm(100), z=rnorm(100), col=factor(rep(1,100)))

p1 <- ggplot(df.d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y, color=col)) + scale_colour_manual(values=c('red'), guide='legend') +ggtitle('Global title')
p2 <- ggplot(df.d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=z, color=col)) + scale_colour_manual(values=c('red'), guide='legend')

gt1 <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p1))
gt2 <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p2))

gt <- gtable(widths = unit(c(4, 4, 1), "null"), heights = unit(c(1, 4), "null"))
gt <- gtable_add_grob(gt, gt1[, -5], t = 2, b = 2, l = 1, r = 1, clip='off')
gt <- gtable_add_grob(gt, gt2[, -5], t = 2, b = 2, l = 2, r = 2, clip='off')
gt <- gtable_add_grob(gt, gtable_filter(gt1, "guide-box"), t = 2, b = 2, l = 3, r = 3, clip='off')

messages.subject: Re: faceting with different data frames
messages.subject_clean: faceting with different data frames
messages.body_plain:
When faceting the facets generally have to have the same x and y axis. If one of your axes is a factor you can have it leave out unused levels per facet or adjust to fit the space if your values per facet are numerically very different, but if you want to facet something that shares an x, but not a y... I'm not sure.

That's probably better done using grid/gridExtra to layout the two plots on top of each other. You could cheat if both Y's are numerical, but then you'd run into issues labeling your y-axis, what units go with which facet?

Perhaps others have better ideas?

B

I wish to have two coordinate systems, one directy above the other (the x axis parallel and identical in terms of sizing). I feel that facet_grid should work (see below - marked with ????) but actually I do not know how to vary the syntay. Could anybody help me?

adata: array data with transcript start sites on chromosome 11 (transcript.start) and the foldchanges.
pdata: histone precipitation data from chromosome 11, start and end are the precipitated DNA coordinates and peak ... the peak.

structure(list(transcript.start = c(3125936L, 3142378L, 3187355L,
3189052L, 3193421L, 3193421L), foldchange = c(0.8656, 0.7751,
0.8779, 0.9557, 1.0108, 0.9307)), .Names = c("transcript.start",

7L)), .Names = c("start", "end", "peak"), row.names = c(NA, 6L
), class = "data.frame")

This is my idea. But: What is the correct syntax for facet_grid?

> p <- ggplot (adata, aes (x=transcript.start, y=foldchange))+ geom_point() + geom_segment (data=pdata, aes (x=start, xend=end, yend=0, y=peak), color="red")

> p+facet_grid()  ?????

Thanks
Hermann

On 10/3/2012 11:10 AM, Ilya wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I'm creating report at work using ggplot2. On first page i put company
> logo/text and when i do that, and save everything in PDF colors on
> following changes loose intensity. Same green color on one page will be
> bright on on next dark. This is example of the code that will produces this
> bug on  my machine. Colors on second and third pages (problems.pdf) will
> look different. Any suggesting on fixing it?
>
> Thank you
>
> library(ggplot2)
> library(scales)
> library(png)
> library(grid)
>
> data.set <-
>    data.frame(year = c(2010, 2010, 2011,2011, 2012, 2012),
>              overtime = c('TRUE', 'FALSE', 'TRUE', 'FALSE', 'TRUE', 'FALSE'),
>              value = c(100, 200, 150, 250, 50, 75))
>
>    logo <-  readPNG(system.file("img", "Rlogo.png", package="png"))
>    logo <- rasterGrob(logo, interpolate=TRUE)
>    title.page <http://title.page> <-
>      qplot(1:10,1:10, geom = 'blank') +
>      annotation_custom(logo, xmin = 0, xmax = 10, ymin = 8, ymax = 10)
>
>
> my.chart.1 <-
>    ggplot(data = data.set,
>           aes(x = overtime,
>               y = value,
>               fill = overtime)) +
>    geom_bar(stat="identity")+
>    scale_fill_manual(values = c('green','red'))
>
> my.chart.2 <-
>    my.chart.1 +
>    facet_wrap(~year)
>
> ## NO PROBLEMS
> pdf(file='no.problems.pdf')
>    print(my.chart.1)
>    print(my.chart.2)
> dev.off()
> ## PROBLEMS WITH COLORS
> pdf(file='problems.pdf')
>    title.page <http://title.page>
>    print(my.chart.1)
>    print(my.chart.2)
> dev.off()
>

I see this behavior as well (R version 2.15.1 (2012-06-22), Platform:
x86_64-pc-mingw32/x64 (64-bit), Adobe Reader version 10.1.4). I don't
know what is causing it, but I might have a workaround and some
additional information.

First, I see the different intensities problem even with pages shuffled:

pdf(file='problems2.pdf')
    print(my.chart.1)
    print(my.chart.2)
    title.page <http://title.page>
dev.off()

It's the inclusion of title.page <http://title.page>, anywhere, that is the problem
(repeating my.chart.1 and my.chart.2 doesn't cause it).

I tried to dive into the PDF's themselves and see what the differences
were, but the compression made it incomprehensible. So I re-created the
PDF's without compression.

pdf(file="problems.pdf", compress=FALSE)
    ...

With this, the colors in "problems.pdf" were darker than in
"no.problems.pdf", but they were consistent! (Both graphs had a darker
green.) So this may be a workaround (though it will make bigger files,
obviously).

I looked at the (not compressed) PDF's and could not see any differences
that lept out at me as causing the differences (additional page graphic
and changes in the object numbers, but nothing related to color I noticed).

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: converting color scale code to the new version of ggplot2
messages.subject_clean: converting color scale code to the new version of ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Following some examples I found on the web, I was able to successfully create some heat maps using ggplot2. Details are here <http://wsuipar.wordpress.com/2012/10/05/where-do-our-students-come-from-with-heat-maps/>. But, before I move on to explore ggmap there's one issue that I was banging my head against that I'd love to see an answer to, just for closure.

The example I was following relied on the previous version of ggplot2 found in R v2.12.2. I couldn't get it to run in the new version of ggplot2 found in 2.15.1. Not for lack of trying, but too much about ggplot2 is a mystery to me right now.

Some code that works in 2.12.1 that contains the basics of what I'm doing is below. The problem is the structure returned by scale_colour_gradient2() and the like has changed. The previous version of that structure contained functions named train() and map() that I was using to create fill values for geom_tile(). But, those aren't available in the new version. I find very little about those two functions looking around, so I expect this was a non-standard technique, so the authors felt safe in abandoning it.

Anyways, does anyone know how to re-write the following so it will produce the same results in the latest version of ggplot2?

Ed

rm(list=ls())
library(MASS)
library(ggplot2)

# data for a base map
PlotData.Base <- data.frame(expand.grid(lat=seq(1, 640), lon=seq(1,640)), fill=rep("#000000", 640*640))

# data for the heat map
DensityList <- kde2d(rnorm(100)*50+320, rnorm(100)*50+320, n = 320, lims = c(c(1,640), c(1,640)))
PlotData.Density <- expand.grid(lon = seq.int <http://seq.int>(1, 640, length.out = 320), lat = seq.int <http://seq.int>(1, 640,  length.out = 320))
PlotData.Density$density <- melt(DensityList$z)$value

# decide what colors to use for the heat map
DensityColorScale <- scale_colour_gradient2(low = 'white', mid = 'red4', high = 'red', midpoint = median(PlotData.Density$density))

# values for alpha to control opacity
PlotData.Density$density0to1  <- pmin(PlotData.Density$density / max(PlotData.Density$density), 0.4 )

#
# these are the problem lines
#
DensityColorScale$train(PlotData.Density$density, T)
PlotData.Density$densityColor <- DensityColorScale$map(PlotData.Density$density)

# plot base map
Plot <- ggplot()
Plot <- Plot + geom_tile(aes(x = lon, y = lat, fill = fill), data = PlotData.Base)
# plot overlay map
Plot   <- Plot + geom_tile(aes(x = lon, y = lat, fill = densityColor, alpha = density0to1), data = PlotData.Density)

print(Plot)

So i still have two questions:

Herbert

        scale_colour_manual(values=c('red'), guide='legend') + theme(legend.position=c(-0.2, 0.6))

p2 <- ggplot(df.d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=z, color=col)) +

        scale_colour_manual(values=c('red'), guide='none')

gt2 <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p2))

gt <- gtable_add_grob(gt, gt2, t = 2, b = 2, l = 2, r = 2, clip='off')

gt <- gtable_add_grob(gt, gtable_filter(gt1, "guide-box"), t = 2, b = 2, l = 3, r = 3, clip='off')

messages.subject: Re: Difficulty graphing with nested data
messages.subject_clean: Difficulty graphing with nested data
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Dodging points, lines and error bars gets rather messy; I'd suggest you consider faceting to ease the computational and visual load. Here are a couple of alternatives; I renamed your data frame dat to avoid potential conflicts with the data() function.

dat <- read.csv("Example_Data.csv", header = TRUE)
library("ggplot2")

ggplot(dat, aes(x = Treatment, y = Mean, colour = Location, shape = Treatment)) +
   theme_bw() +
   geom_point() +
   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Mean - ci, ymax = Mean + ci), colour = "black",
                    width = 0.1) +
   geom_line(aes(group = Location)) +
   labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Mean Time (Hours)", colour = "Location",
        title = "Effect of treatment \nin different populations") +
   theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) +
   facet_wrap(~ Generation, nrow = 1)

ggplot(dat, aes(x = Location, y = Mean, colour = Treatment, shape = Treatment)) +
   theme_bw() +
   geom_point() +
   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Mean - ci, ymax = Mean + ci), colour = "black",
                    width = 0.1) +
   geom_line(aes(group = Treatment)) +
   labs(x = "Location", y = "Mean Time (Hours)", colour = "Treatment",
        title = "Effect of treatment \nin different populations") +
   theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) +
   coord_flip() +
   facet_wrap(~ Generation, ncol = 1)

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Sorry for the late reply on this - I've spent the past two weeks packing and moving and am finally starting to get some energy back.

On Sat, Sep 22, 2012 at 10:33 AM, Joshua Wiley <jwiley...@gmail.com> wrote:
> A few suggestions:
>
> 1) Include a link on how to install R or get R.  I say this because I
> think that ggplot2 has grown large enough people may find it before
> they find R---that is they may see a cool graphic, see that it was
> made in ggplot2 and then want to learn more.
> 2) I think it would be great to have a list of resources for learning
> ggplot2 up on the main website.  Off the top of my head, Dennis'
> transition guide and the theme guide either as webpages or PDFs would
> be good.  What I would really love is something like Hadley's ggplot2
> book, but available all online (and updated for the most recent
> version of ggplot2).  Perhaps this could be something on github that
> the community could help with the maintenance of and then is just
> periodically checked and built for the website.

There is an e-book project afoot whose purpose is to replace and update Hadley's 2009 book with more examples, but to avoid copyright issues, it has to be rewritten more or less from scratch. The new theme system tome is to be the first major contribution to that project, the next being all the changes around scales and the gtable package, the latter of which I have to admit is rather opaque to me at the moment. Fortunately, some folks have been posting code recently so I have a chance to see how it works by example. It'll be a few months before all of this has a definite shape.

At the same time, the other features of the package, from philosophy to implementation, need to be addressed as well in order to achieve a complete reference. For example, I'm thinking about a chapter that would more or less be a walkthrough of what is going on underneath the hood when a ggplot is constructed with two layers and then several layers.

Winston's forthcoming book (R Graphics Cookbook) covers a number of practical problems in a clear, organized way, but it's somewhere between a tutorial and the e-book in progress. It has its own important niche in the documentation stream.

>
> I work at a university statistical consulting center that has
> traditionally focused primarily on supporting Stata, SAS, and SPSS.  I
> have been putting a lot of work into expanding the resources we have
> available for R in person and on our (freely available) website and I
> make heavy use of ggplot2 for data exploration and presentation of
> model results (e.g., http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/R/dae/ztnb.htm).
> However, I do not really have good resources to _introduce_ ggplot2.
> If I could say, "There are a couple great guides and introductions to
> ggplot2 as well as all the documentation on its website, ggplot2.org <http://ggplot2.org>"
> that would be fantastic.  I think a lot of the clients I see are
> impressed with the graphs, but feel overwhelmed to do it themselves.
> Final products are great for display, but poor for teaching.

You've done a great job incorporating R into those lovely practical examples (thanks!!). Here are a few simple ggplot2 tutorials that I scared up with a Google search:

http://www.ceb-institute.org/bbs/wp-content/uploads/2011/09/handout_ggplot2.pdf
https://github.com/echen/ggplot2-tutorial
http://www.columbia.edu/~cjd11/charles_dimaggio/DIRE/resources/R/ggplotTutorial.pdf

...and the very well done tutorial from Penn for which I had to search a little harder...
http://www.ling.upenn.edu/~joseff/rstudy/summer2010_ggplot2_intro.html

I didn't read over these tutorials in any great depth so I don't know how up to date they are. From skimming them, it appears that the Penn page is probably the closest to what I would consider a comprehensive tutorial on ggplot2, but it's missing a few things, too.

It would be nice to have an 'official' ggplot2 tutorial, I suppose, although I tend to think of the qplot chapter in Hadley's book as the canonical introduction to the package. It might be worthwhile to brainstorm on the ggplot2-dev group (and perhaps here, where more novices are likely to tune in) as to what such an animal might look like. I don't mind organizing the effort until it takes shape and others can take over, but I probably won't have the time to do most of the writing as I need to be focused elsewhere.

I would suggest that the ggplot2 chapter in Paul Murrell's R Graphics 2e be a guidepost of sorts, as he nailed the central principles of the package. The concepts are to be discussed more fully in the e-book, but examples that illustrate the core principles would be very useful to beginners IMO.

Dennis

> community.  In addition to his own amazing work, Hadley has managed to

messages.subject_clean: ggsave with multiple plots - only final plot saved
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I have arranged two plots into one window using multiplot(), see link below. When I save this using ggsave(), it only saves the final plot. Using pdf() ... dev.off() works fine.  Is there a way to do this fully within ggplot2?

MWE:
library(ggplot2)
# require: load multiplot() from: http://wiki.stdout.org/rcookbook/Graphs/Multiple%20graphs%20on%20one%20page%20(ggplot2)/
dat <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 1:10)
p1 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point(col="black", size = 4)
p2 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point(col="red", size = 4)
multiplot(p1, p2)
ggsave("test1.pdf")    #Only saves p2
pdf("test2.pdf")
multiplot(p1, p2)
dev.off()                   #Saves everything - but seems a bit hacky

Added info: the plots are not saved on multiple pages, there really is just one plot. I guess it's because ggsave grabs "last_plot()", and multiplot plots each element separately.

Thanks!
Benjamin

Sadly, this doesn't work with ggsave currently because it will simply take the last plot in your case p2 and then plot it. It does not recognize grid object that is assembled by multiplot(). When you save you will have to do what you've been doing png()/pdf(); dev.off() for the foreseeable future. There have been mutterings that the ability to do what you want is on the way, but I think it is fairly low priority at the moment.

messages.subject: Re: use ggplot2 boxplot to show linear correlation between several variable to one variables
messages.subject_clean: use ggplot2 boxplot to show linear correlation between several variable to one variables
messages.body_plain:
I think you'll want everything in a single data frame; compute the R2
values using something like ddply; and then plot the resulting data
frame. For example:

# Here's your data in a single data frame
d <- structure(list(Date = structure(c(2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 4L), .Label
= c("1//3/2012",
"1/1/12", "1/2/12", "1/3/12"), class = "factor"), Variable = structure(c(1L,
1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L), .Label = c("CPU", "Memory"), class = "factor"),
    Value = c(10L, 20L, 30L, 20L, 3L, 80L), Number_Outages = c(0L,
    1L, 2L, 0L, 0L, 2L)), .Names = c("Date", "Variable", "Value",
"Number_Outages"), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA, -6L))

# Compute the summary data frame
library(plyr)
d_smry <- ddply(d,.(Variable),.fun=function(x){return(c("Cor"=cor(x$Value,x$Number_Outages)))})

# and plot it
library(ggplot2)
qplot(Variable,Cor,data=d_smry,geom="bar")

Ben

Currently from your data (the example you sent) you'll only get one R2
per variable. If you have more than one (that is, if there's another
variable you're subsetting by, so that you'll have multiple
correlation values), then absolutely, use a boxplot + coord_flip() and

messages.subject: Re: How to get rid of default grey background color in a lineplot legend
messages.subject_clean: How to get rid of default grey background color in a lineplot legend
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

for me, this worked...

#removing background

p + theme(
+     panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent",colour =
NA), # or theme_blank()
+     panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
+     panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
+     plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent",colour =
NA)) + xlim=c(1,12)

Cheers
Jo

You're trying to reorder a factor, which doesn't giving the expected
results. Before your call to ggplot change 'country' to character:

d$country <- as.character(d$country)

messages.subject: Parsed labels in facet_grid
messages.subject_clean: Parsed labels in facet_grid
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I try to do a facet plot and want to rename the labels of the
facets. I tried to follow the describtion at
http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/facet_grid.html
but I can'T get it work properly. In my case it is a mix of normal
text (with space) and math expression such as m^2. How can that be achieved?

I modify my variable labels with:
df$var <- factor(df$var, labels = c("W A [m^2]", "WUA [m^2]", "HHS"))

and try to plot the new labels with:
facet_grid(..., labeller = label_parsed)

Any suggestions to solve that?

Thanks,

Johannes

messages.subject: Re: How to get rid of default grey background color in a lineplot legend
messages.subject_clean: How to get rid of default grey background color in a lineplot legend
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jo,
while this deletes the background for me, the grey in the legend is still there:

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-9JWdz0JD6WQ/UHl3JP4EKDI/AAAAAAAAAEQ/fx7ck_YkmzI/s1600/Screen+Shot+2012-10-13+at+4.12.53+PM.PNG>

p + geom_line(aes(linetype = factor(Rd), group = factor(Rd)))  + theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent",colour = NA), plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent",colour = NA), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent",colour = NA))

I am using version 0.9.2.1 on a mac.

Greetings,

Jan

On Thursday, October 11, 2012 7:20:37 PM UTC+2, Johannes Björk wrote:
> Hi,
>
> for me, this worked...
>
> #removing background
>
> p + theme(
> +     panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent",colour =
> NA), # or theme_blank()
> +     panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
> +     panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
> +     plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent",colour =
> NA)) + xlim=c(1,12)
>
> Cheers
> Jo
>
> On 11 oct, 16:07, Jannemann <janheusch...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hello together,
> > I was looking all over the place but I can't figure out how to get rid of
> > the default grey background color in a lineplot legend. I tried to set the
> > plot and the panel background to blank but with no success. Can this be
> > done in ggplot2?
> > Thanks in advance for your help.
> >
> > Here is a small reproducable example:
> >
> > #This generates a small dataset
> > h = 240
> > R = seq(0.1,0.5,by=0.1)
> > d = seq(0.0,2.0, by=0.1)
> > Rd = rep(R, length(d))
> > dd = rep(d, each = length(R))
> > FSea = Rd * 2 * 0.03
> > Er = FSea*dd / (1 + FSea*h*dd)
> >
> > dset = data.frame(cbind(Er,dd,Rd))
> >
> > #Some theme elements
> > graph1 = theme(aspect.ratio = 1, panel.background = element_blank(),
> > axis.line = element_line(), panel.grid.minor =
> > element_blank(),panel.grid.major = element_blank(), plot.background =
> > element_blank())
> >
> > p = ggplot(data = dset, aes(x = dd, y = (Er*3600)))
> > p + geom_line(aes(linetype = factor(Rd), group = factor(Rd))) +
> > scale_x_continuous("Density") + scale_y_continuous("Encounters") +
> > guides(linetype = guide_legend("Reaction")) +
> > theme(legend.position=c(0.85,0.35), panel.background = element_blank()) +
> > graph1

messages.body_plain:
In the geom_abline documentation:

  http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/geom_abline.html

it lists alpha, colour, linetype, size as the only aesthetics but then in the examples there is an example where slope and intercept are aesthetics:

  # Slopes and intercepts as data
  p <- ggplot <http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/ggplot.html>(mtcars, aes <http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/aes.html>(x = wt, y=mpg), . ~ cyl) + geom_point <http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/geom_point.html>()
  df <- data.frame <http://www.inside-r.org/r-doc/base/data.frame>(a=rnorm <http://www.inside-r.org/r-doc/stats/Normal>(10, 25), b=rnorm <http://www.inside-r.org/r-doc/stats/Normal>(10, 0))
  p + geom_abline <http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/geom_abline.html>(aes <http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/aes.html>(intercept=a, slope=b), data=df)

I was thinking that this might be an error in the documentation but then I noticed in the source this line in geom-abline.r :

  default_aes <- function(.) aes(colour="black", size=0.5, linetype=1, alpha = NA)

which also lists alpha, colour, linetype and size as the only aesthetics.

Are intercept and slope supposed to be aesthetics and if they are is this an error in the documentation and in the source?

messages.subject: plotting specaccum{vegan} objects in ggplot2?
messages.subject_clean: plotting specaccum{vegan} objects in ggplot2?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

has anyone out there plotted 'specaccum' and 'fitspecaccum' objects from
{vegan} with ggplot2 and would be willing to share some experience (and
code)?

I am posting some examples below, including a plot via
plotspecaccum{BiodiversityR} which I would like to rebuild in ggplot2.

Cheers,
a+

################################################################
library(vegan)
data(dune.env)
data(dune)

acc <- specaccum(dune, method="random", permutations=2)
# Low nr. of permutations just to check the structure!
str(acc)
# adds arrhenius (power) models to the randomized SACurves:
mod <- fitspecaccum(acc, "arrh")
class(mod)
str(mod) # very complicated stucture!
# plots the specaccum-object:
plot(acc)
# plots the nlm's:
plot(mod, col=rgb(255,0,0,50, maxColorValue=255), add=TRUE)
# gives number of model with best AIC:
best <- which((sapply(mod$models, AIC)) == min(sapply(mod$models, AIC)))
# summarizes the best model, including k and z values.
mod$models[best]

############################################################
# Plotting a single nl-model from fitspeccaccum{vegan} is complictated,
# this is only a quick-and-dirty workaround:
# (first, include more permutations!)
acc <- specaccum(dune, method="random", permutations=100)
mod <- fitspecaccum(acc, "arrh")

plot(acc)
plot(mod, col=rgb(0,0,255,20, maxColorValue=255), add=TRUE)

best <- which((sapply(mod$models, AIC)) == min(sapply(mod$models, AIC)))
# workaround to get the best model out of the object:
# recycle, to get a plottable object of the class speccacum:
workaround <- acc
# replace y-values with model fit:
workaround$richness <- mod$fitted[,best]
plot(workaround, col=rgb(255,0,0,150, maxColorValue=255), add=TRUE)

#### Some plots I'd like to rebuild using ggplot2:
plot(acc, ci.type="polygon", col=rgb(1,1,1), lwd=1, ci.lty=0,
ci.col=rgb(150,150,180,127, maxColorValue=255))
plot(workaround, add=TRUE, col=rgb(255,0,0,50, maxColorValue=255), lwd=2)
plot(workaround, ci.type="polygon", col=rgb(1,1,1), lwd=1, ci.lty=0,
ci.col=rgb(1,1,1,70, maxColorValue=255), add=TRUE)
mod$models[best]
# Side problem: how to access z-values from the object?
str(mod$models[best]) # It's a list!
#######################################################

################################################################################
# Approach of data handling using factors which I need to rebuild:
library(BiodiversityR)
accumcomp(dune, y=dune.env, factor="Management", method="exact",
permutations=100)

messages.body_plain:
Hi - Please see sample code. I am trying to plot a barchart of a simple timeseries. Barcharts produce unnecessary spacing for weekends, in order to counter that I make my x axis as a character. however on doing that the labels on the x axis are not correct (showing jan dates instead of october). Any advice?

tS = timeSequence(from = paste('2010', "-10-01", sep = ""),to = paste('2010', "-10-30", sep = ""))
dates <-as.Date(as.character(tS[which(!isWeekend(tS))]))
values <- c(1:NROW(dates))
mydata <- data.frame(dates, values)

# -- plot in date format
ggplot(mydata, aes(x=dates, y=values)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") + scale_x_date(major = '1 week')

# -- dates in character, fixes the spacing issue but now the x axis labels are messed up
mydata2 <-data.frame(as.character(dates), values)
colnames(mydata2) <- c('dates', 'values')
ggplot(mydata2, aes(x=dates, y=values)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity")
ggplot(mydata2, aes(x=dates, y=values)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") + scale_x_date(major = '1 week')

On 10/15/2012 11:46 AM, rb wrote:
> Hi - Please see sample code. I am trying to plot a barchart of a simple
> timeseries. Barcharts produce unnecessary spacing for weekends, in order to
> counter that I make my x axis as a character. however on doing that the
> labels on the x axis are not correct (showing jan dates instead of
> october). Any advice?

Its' worth pointing out timeSequence is in the timeDate pacakge

> tS = timeSequence(from = paste('2010', "-10-01", sep = ""),to =
> paste('2010', "-10-30", sep = ""))
> dates <-as.Date(as.character(tS[which(!isWeekend(tS))]))
> values <- c(1:NROW(dates))
> mydata <- data.frame(dates, values)
>
> # -- plot in date format
> ggplot(mydata, aes(x=dates, y=values)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
> scale_x_date(major = '1 week')
>
> # -- dates in character, fixes the spacing issue but now the x axis labels
> are messed up
> mydata2 <-data.frame(as.character(dates), values)
> colnames(mydata2) <- c('dates', 'values')
> ggplot(mydata2, aes(x=dates, y=values)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity")
> ggplot(mydata2, aes(x=dates, y=values)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
> scale_x_date(major = '1 week')

I don't see dates from January; I still see dates in October.  The last
of these two won't work because the x-axis is now character (discrete),
not date.

Using

ggplot(mydata2, aes(x=dates, y=values)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity")

I get labels "2010-10-01", "2010-10-04", "2010-10-05", etc., in various
amounts of overlap (depending on how big I make the window).  I can
rotate the labels to make them easier to read

ggplot(mydata2, aes(x=dates, y=values)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") +

theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=90, vjust=0.5))

Or, since it seems you are using an older version of ggplot2,

ggplot(mydata2, aes(x=dates, y=values)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") +

opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=90))

Why do you think the dates are in January?

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: axis labels in 10^x format in ggplot 0.9.2.1
messages.subject_clean: axis labels in 10^x format in ggplot 0.9.2.1
messages.body_plain:
Previous to ggplot 0.9 I used to use this function to convert number formats on axis labels to scientific 10^x format (10'superscript'x)
myfmt <- function(x, ...)
   format(x, big.mark = '', trim = TRUE, scientific = TRUE, ...)

and then used the `formatter` option in scale_continuous to call it
scale_y_continuous(formatter = myfmt)

As of V0.9 formatter has been disabled in the new scales package.

Scales allows producing labels of the type `1ex` using:
scale_y_continuous(labels = scientific_format())
But no option produces the 10^x format

And ggplot2_0.9.0_changes describes how to get it for a log transformed axis
scale_y_log10old <- function(...) {
scale_y_log10(breaks = trans_breaks('log10', function(x) 10^x),
labels = trans_format('log10', math_format(10^.x)), ...)
}

But I couldn't figure out how to get it to work on a continuous axis, i.e. simply display '1000' as '10^3' without transforming anything.

This is most likely been answered somewhere already but I just couldn't find it anywhere.

Roey

messages.subject_clean: plot histogram or some other geom on ggmap object
messages.body_plain:
Yea, I'm not sure if I understand the question correctly.  But if you'd like to use ggmap and ggsubplot, here's a basic example I cooked up based on Garrett's; I haven't played around with it very much though.

I think you'll need to think about what you want your aesthetics to be, remembering that geom_bar defaults to stat_bin as opposed to stat_identity.  For more on that, see http://docs.ggplot2.org/0.9.2.1/.

Cheers
david.

library(ggsubplot)
library(ggmap)

qmap('afghanistan', zoom = 6, maptype = 'toner', extent = 'panel') +
  geom_subplot2d(
    aes(lon, lat,
      subplot = geom_bar(aes(victim, ..count.., fill = victim))
    ), bins = c(15,12), ref = NULL, width = rel(0.8),
    data = casualties
  )

Are the values counts (= positive integers)? In that case a poisson regression is more suitable as smoother. E.g. geom_smooth(method = 'glm', family = 'poisson')

set.seed(12345)
library(ggplot2)
library(mgcv)
Dataset <- data.frame(A = seq(-10, 10, length = 1001))
Dataset$B <- rpois(nrow(Dataset),  exp(2 + 0.1 * Dataset$A - 0.1 * Dataset$A ^ 2))
ggplot(Dataset, aes(x = A, y = B)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth()
ggplot(Dataset, aes(x = A, y = B)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "glm", family = "poisson")
ggplot(Dataset, aes(x = A, y = B)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "glm", family = "poisson", formula = y ~ poly(x, 2))
ggplot(Dataset, aes(x = A, y = B)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "gam", family = "poisson")
ggplot(Dataset, aes(x = A, y = B)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "gam", family = "poisson", formula = y ~ s(x))

ggplot(Dataset, aes(x = A, y = B)) + geom_smooth(method = "gam", family = "poisson", formula = y ~ s(x)) + coord_cartesian(ylim = (c(-0.1, 1))) #note that even the confidence intervals are non-negative

messages.subject: Re: axis labels in 10^x format in ggplot 0.9.2.1
messages.subject_clean: axis labels in 10^x format in ggplot 0.9.2.1
messages.body_plain:
On 10/17/2012 6:48 AM, Brandon Hurr wrote:
> Can you tell I don't usually mess with scales?
>
> You might have to make your own trans formatter again...
>
> ?scales::trans_new

It is "simpler" than that. You don't need to create a transformation,
just a function that formats the labels (as already determined) into
what is desired. That is, you just need a labels function. This one will
work:

fancy_scientific <- function(l) {
     # turn in to character string in scientific notation
     l <- format(l, scientific = TRUE)
     # quote the part before the exponent to keep all the digits
     l <- gsub("^(.*)e", "'\\1'e", l)
     # turn the 'e+' into plotmath format
     l <- gsub("e", "%*%10^", l)
     # return this as an expression
     parse(text=l)
}

Which you can then use as

ggplot(data=df, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
   geom_point() +
   scale_x_continuous(labels=fancy_scientific)

This may not be exactly what you want; it displays 0 as 0.0 x 10^+0 and
1000 as 1.0 x 10^+4. If you want something different, then you have to
pull the relevant parts out from a vector of positions and assemble the
expressions yourself.

messages.subject: Stacking order
messages.subject_clean: Stacking order
messages.body_plain:
I am not sure if this a bug of a feature, but I found an inconsistency in the stacking order, depending of the geometry being used. In the example below color/fill are based on a factor. geom_bar uses the levels of the factor to create the stacking order, while the rest do it alphabetically.

I run into this issue when I was trying to make a stacked area plot. I know I can fix the order manually, but I was wondering if the order should be consistent across geometries.

I am running R 1.15.1 and ggplot2 v0.9.2.1.

Thanks for your time,
Eduardo

___________________________

library(ggplot2)
data <- data.frame(
        g = rep(LETTERS[1:3], each=4),
        x = rep(1:4, 3),
        y = 1:12)
data$g <- factor(data$g, levels = c("B", "C", "A"))

# Bars ordered following the levels in the factor
ggplot(data, aes(x = x, weight = y, fill = g)) + geom_bar(binwidth = 0.5)

# Stacking order alphabetically
ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = g)) + geom_area()
ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y, color = g)) + geom_line(position = "stack")
ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y, color = g)) + geom_point(position = "stack")

# Stacking following the levels (like geom_bar)
ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = g, order = as.numeric(g))) + geom_area()
ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y, color = g, order = as.numeric(g))) + geom_line(position = "stack")
ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y, color = g, order = as.numeric(g))) + geom_point(position = "stack")

messages.subject_clean: Adding annotations across faceted plots
messages.body_plain:
You can create a separate dataframe with your labels/annotations, and that dataframe will have to have the same levels as the facets. Something like the following:

ggplot()+
geom_point(data=df, aes(x=x, y=y, color=groupingvar1)+
geom_text(data=label.df, aes(x=-Inf, y=-Inf)+
facet_wrap(.~groupingvar2)

B

- the plotting region for p2

messages.subject: Presenting ggmcmc
messages.subject_clean: Presenting ggmcmc
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

We have another ggplot2 creature with us. Let me present you ggmcmc, an R
package for visual MCMC convergence and diagnostics, which tries to make
life easier by plotting all convergence plots in a single pdf file for a
more convenient inspection.

ggmcmc is a set of tools for assessing and diagnosing convergence
of Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations, as well as for graphically display
results from full MCMC analysis:
http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggmcmc/index.html

There is a tutorial showing the possibilities of ggmcmc at
http://xavier-fim.net/packages/ggmcmc

It is still under development and I am plannig it to extend it, so it would
be great if you can test it and tell me whether it is useful or not, or any
other idea that you want to share.
https://github.com/xfim/ggmcmc

Best,
--
-  Xavier  -

messages.subject: how to use geom_text in combination with geom_violin, when position="dodge"?
messages.subject_clean: how to use geom_text in combination with geom_violin, when position="dodge"?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I have a violin plot where, for each x, there are different figures, coloured according to another variable and positioned using position="dodge".
This can be explained better with some code:

   # reduce the size of the diamonds dataset, for faster debugging

   diamonds.short = subset(diamonds, cut == "Premium" & x > 7)
   # plot violin plots
   ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price)) + geom_violin(aes(color=color))

On this plot, I want to add some text labels, showing the price of all the diamonds that have a value of "x" higher than 9.

This is how it should look like:
- http://bioevo.upf.edu/~gdallolio/images/ggplot_question_wanted.png
However, this is what I have obtained so far:
- http://bioevo.upf.edu/~gdallolio/images/ggplot_question_obtained.png

Complete code:

   library(ggplot2)
   diamonds.short = subset(diamonds, cut == "Premium" & x > 7)
   ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price)) + geom_violin(aes(color=color)) + geom_text(data=subset(diamonds.short, x>9), aes(label=carat))

Each of the  text labels should be showed inside the violin plot where they belong. For example, if the diamond that has (price = 2.71) belongs to "E" color, its label should be shown inside the E figure.

I suspect that the solution lays in giving a correct value of "position" to geom_text, but so far I could not find the correct way.
This is what I have tried so far, but none of these work:
   library(ggplot2)

   diamonds.short = subset(diamonds, cut == "Premium" & x > 7)
   ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price)) + geom_violin(aes(color=color)) + geom_text(data=subset(diamonds.short, x>9), aes(label=carat, color=color), position="dodge")

   ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price)) +
geom_violin(aes(color=color)) + geom_text(data=subset(diamonds.short,
x>9), aes(label=carat, color=color, position=color))
   ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price)) +
geom_violin(aes(color=color)) + geom_text(data=subset(diamonds.short,
x>9), aes(label=carat, color=color), position=position_dodge(width=0.9))
   ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price)) +
geom_violin(aes(color=color)) + geom_text(data=subset(diamonds.short,
x>9), aes(label=carat, color=color), position=position_identity(width=0.9))

The best I was able to do so is to paste cut and color into a new column, and use that for scale_x:
    diamonds.short$cut_color = paste(diamonds.short$cut, diamonds.short$color, sep='_')
    ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut_color, y=price)) + geom_violin(aes(color=color)) + geom_text(data=subset(diamonds.short, x>9), aes(label=carat, color=color))

The problem is that now I don't know how to remove the extra labels on the X axis. Plus, I think that there is should be some better way to do this, using position.

What is the best ggplot2-ish way to do this? How can I plot the labels on the correct violin?

Thanks,
Gio
--
Giovanni Dall'Olio, phd student

IBE, Institut de Biologia Evolutiva, CEXS-UPF (Barcelona, Spain)

My blog on bioinformatics: http://bioinfoblog.it

messages.subject: Re: date in qplot()
messages.subject_clean: date in qplot()
messages.body_plain:
Luo,

there's a couple of things that you need to take care of, before your chart will work.
First, you'll have to work on the YearQuarter variable - split it in pieces along the white space (look into strsplit) to get Year and Month out.
Then pieve them together into a proper date (look into the package lubridate)
In your line chart you need to set a different grouping variable. You seem to be grouping by YearQuarter at the moment, hence the vertical lines. Instead, identify what the lines have in common across time (is it Provider or Type or both?). Use the grouping variable for that, and you should be getting closer to what you want to show,

HTH,

Heike

messages.subject: Re: how to use geom_text in combination with geom_violin, when position="dodge"?
messages.subject_clean: how to use geom_text in combination with geom_violin, when position="dodge"?
messages.body_plain:
On 10/22/2012 6:08 AM, Giovanni Marco Dall'Olio wrote:
> Hello,
> I have a violin plot where, for each x, there are different figures,
> coloured according to another variable and positioned using
> position="dodge".
> This can be explained better with some code:
>
>     # reduce the size of the diamonds dataset, for faster debugging
>     diamonds.short = subset(diamonds, cut == "Premium" & x > 7)
>     # plot violin plots
>     ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price)) +
> geom_violin(aes(color=color))
>
>
> On this plot, I want to add some text labels, showing the price of all the
> diamonds that have a value of "x" higher than 9.
> This is how it should look like:
> - http://bioevo.upf.edu/~gdallolio/images/ggplot_question_wanted.png
> However, this is what I have obtained so far:
> - http://bioevo.upf.edu/~gdallolio/images/ggplot_question_obtained.png
>
> Complete code:
>
>     library(ggplot2)
>     diamonds.short = subset(diamonds, cut == "Premium" & x > 7)
>     ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price)) +
> geom_violin(aes(color=color)) + geom_text(data=subset(diamonds.short, x>9),
> aes(label=carat))
>
> Each of the text labels should be showed inside the violin plot where they
> belong. For example, if the diamond that has (price = 2.71) belongs to "E"
> color, its label should be shown inside the E figure.
>
> I suspect that the solution lays in giving a correct value of "position" to
> geom_text, but so far I could not find the correct way.
> This is what I have tried so far, but none of these work:
>     library(ggplot2)
>     diamonds.short = subset(diamonds, cut == "Premium" & x > 7)
>     ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price)) +
> geom_violin(aes(color=color)) + geom_text(data=subset(diamonds.short, x>9),
> aes(label=carat, color=color), position="dodge")
>     ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price)) +
> geom_violin(aes(color=color)) + geom_text(data=subset(diamonds.short, x>9),
> aes(label=carat, color=color, position=color))
>     ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price)) +
> geom_violin(aes(color=color)) + geom_text(data=subset(diamonds.short, x>9),
> aes(label=carat, color=color), position=position_dodge(width=0.9))
>     ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price)) +
> geom_violin(aes(color=color)) + geom_text(data=subset(diamonds.short, x>9),
> aes(label=carat, color=color), position=position_identity(width=0.9))

The problem you are running into might be a bug, but I can explain what
is happening.  First, this is what should work:

ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price, color=color)) +
   geom_violin() +
   geom_text(data=diamonds.short[diamonds.short[["x"]] > 9,],
aes(label=carat),
     position=position_dodge(width=0.9))

It doesn't, and the reason it doesn't is that there is no color=="D"
that also has x>9. So that combination is empty in your subset and the
labels then get spread across 6 different groups/positions rather than
7. You can see this by changing the threshold such that there is a D
which meets criteria; the labels align correctly:

ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price, color=color)) +
   geom_violin() +
   geom_text(data=diamonds.short[diamonds.short[["x"]] > 8.98,],
aes(label=carat),
     position=position_dodge(width=0.9))

A workaround is to create a separation annotation dataset which has
dummy, missing entries for all the levels:

bigs <- diamonds.short[diamonds.short[["x"]] > 9,]
bigs <- rbind.fill(bigs, data.frame(color = levels(bigs$color),
cut="Premium"))

I have to include the color, since that is what I need one of, and cut
because that is the x variable. Now I can use this dataset in the
geom_text call and it aligns correctly:

ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut, y=price, color=color)) +
   geom_violin() +
   geom_text(data=bigs, aes(label=carat),
     position=position_dodge(width=0.9))

> The best I was able to do so is to paste cut and color into a new column,
> and use that for scale_x:
>      diamonds.short$cut_color = paste(diamonds.short$cut,
> diamonds.short$color, sep='_')
>      ggplot(data=diamonds.short, aes(x=cut_color, y=price)) +
> geom_violin(aes(color=color)) + geom_text(data=subset(diamonds.short, x>9),
> aes(label=carat, color=color))
>
> The problem is that now I don't know how to remove the extra labels on the
> X axis.

You could take this approach by specifying the breaks and associated
levels.

+ scale_x_discrete(breaks="Premium_G", labels="Premium")

 > Plus, I think that there is should be some better way to do this,
> using position.
>
> What is the best ggplot2-ish way to do this? How can I plot the labels on
> the correct violin?
> Thanks,
> Gio

--

Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

Luo,

there's a couple of things that you need to take care of, before your chart will work.

First, you'll have to work on the YearQuarter variable - split it in pieces along the white space (look into strsplit) to get Year and Month out.

Then pieve them together into a proper date (look into the package lubridate)

In your line chart you need to set a different grouping variable. You seem to be grouping by YearQuarter at the moment, hence the vertical lines. Instead, identify what the lines have in common across time (is it Provider or Type or both?). Use the grouping variable for that, and you should be getting closer to what you want to show,

HTH,

Heike

mydf <- data.frame(
        provider = rep(letters[1:4], 20),
        quart = seq(from = as.Date("2011-09-01"), to = as.Date("2011-09-30"), length.out = 20),
        customers = runif(20) * 200)
head(mydf)

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(mydf, aes(x = quart, y = customers)) + geom_line() + facet_wrap(~ provider)

Cheers,
Roman

Luo,

there's a couple of things that you need to take care of, before your chart will work.

First, you'll have to work on the YearQuarter variable - split it in pieces along the white space (look into strsplit) to get Year and Month out.

Then pieve them together into a proper date (look into the package lubridate)

In your line chart you need to set a different grouping variable. You seem to be grouping by YearQuarter at the moment, hence the vertical lines. Instead, identify what the lines have in common across time (is it Provider or Type or both?). Use the grouping variable for that, and you should be getting closer to what you want to show,

HTH,

Heike

messages.body_plain:
Dear Community,

I need only a final adivce to be happy with my figures...

1.) I create three figures: (like following)

bi42<-ggplot(reg1_42,aes(treat,biov,fill=treat))+geom_boxplot(fill=c("white","grey60","grey80"),width=0.8,size=0.8, colour="black")+
  theme_bw()+
  xlab("Treatments")+
  ylab(expression(paste(log~biovolume~"[",µm^3~L^-1,"]")))+
  annotate("text",size=8,x=2,y=18.64,label="a")+
  annotate("text",size=8,x=1,y=19.1,label="b")+
  annotate("text",size=8,x=3,y=19.14,label="b")+
  theme(axis.text.x=element_blank(),axis.title.x=element_blank())+
  theme(axis.text.y=element_text(size=14,colour="black",face="bold"),axis.title.y=element_text(size=18,colour="black",vjust=0.3))+
  geom_segment(data=whiskers,aes(x=as.numeric(treat)-0.1,y=lower,xend=as.numeric(treat)+0.1,yend=lower),size=0.8)+
  geom_segment(data=whiskers,aes(x=as.numeric(treat)-0.1,y=upper,xend=as.numeric(treat)+0.1,yend=upper),size=0.8)+
  theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+
  theme(panel.border=element_rect(size=1.5,colour="black"))+
  theme(axis.ticks.length=unit(0.3,"cm"))+
  theme(axis.ticks=element_line(size=1.2))

ri42<-ggplot(reg1_42,aes(treat,rich,fill=treat))+geom_boxplot(fill=c("white","grey60","grey80"),width=0.8,size=0.8, colour="black")+
  theme_bw()+
  ylab("Species richness")+
  theme(axis.text.x=element_blank(),axis.title.x=element_blank())+
  theme(axis.text.y=element_text(size=14,colour="black",face="bold"),axis.title.y=element_text(size=18,colour="black",vjust=0.3))+
  geom_segment(data=whiskers1,aes(x=as.numeric(treat)-0.1,y=lower,xend=as.numeric(treat)+0.1,yend=lower),size=0.8)+
  geom_segment(data=whiskers1,aes(x=as.numeric(treat)-0.1,y=upper,xend=as.numeric(treat)+0.1,yend=upper),size=0.8)+
  theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+
  theme(panel.border=element_rect(size=1.5,colour="black"))+
  theme(axis.ticks.length=unit(0.3,"cm"))+
  theme(axis.ticks=element_line(size=1.2))

ev42<-ggplot(reg1_42,aes(treat,even,fill=treat))+geom_boxplot(fill=c("white","grey60","grey80"),width=0.8,size=0.8, colour="black")+
  theme_bw()+
  xlab("Treatments")+
  ylab("Evenness")+
  annotate("text",size=8,x=1,y=0.665,label="a")+
  annotate("text",size=8,x=2,y=0.778,label="b")+
  annotate("text",size=8,x=3,y=0.768,label="ab")+
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(size=14,colour="black",face="bold"),axis.title.x=element_text(size=18,colour="black",vjust=0.1))+
  theme(axis.text.y=element_text(size=14,colour="black",face="bold"),axis.title.y=element_text(size=18,colour="black",vjust=0.3))+
  geom_segment(data=whiskers2,aes(x=as.numeric(treat)-0.1,y=lower,xend=as.numeric(treat)+0.1,yend=lower),size=0.8)+
  geom_segment(data=whiskers2,aes(x=as.numeric(treat)-0.1,y=upper,xend=as.numeric(treat)+0.1,yend=upper),size=0.8)+
  theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+
  theme(panel.border=element_rect(size=1.5,colour="black"))+
  theme(axis.ticks.length=unit(0.3,"cm"))+
  theme(axis.ticks=element_line(size=1.2))+
  geom_segment(aes(x=2,y=0.5966,xend=2,yend=0.4853),size=0.5)

And than I used grid.arrange (bi42,ri42,ev42) to plot them on one page: (see above)

My Problem is now:

How can I align the y-axis + title (left side) of all three plots, that they are exactly on top of each other? (In the moment they are y-axis title aligned)
Shall I change the xlim or plot.size?

Thanks in advance
Nils

messages.body_plain:
ok- so i've found some nice code to construct a forest plot (below)- but i want to display different sets of coefficients from  multiple models using facets- so i want d$x to index treatment effect or interaction, d$y as my coefficients expressed as odds ratios, and d$ylo /d$yhi as my upper and lower cis, then i want to use facet grid to display the treatment effect and treatment+interaction effect for e.g. seven outcomes (d$outcome) and seven  individual covariates (d$covar)

anyone want to help?

# d is a data frame with 4 columns
# d$x gives variable names
# d$y gives center point
# d$ylo gives lower limits
# d$yhi gives upper limits
forestplot <- function(d, xlab="Odds Ratio", ylab="Study"){
    require(ggplot2)
    p <- ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y=y, ymin=ylo, ymax=yhi)) +
		geom_pointrange() +
		coord_flip() +
		geom_hline(aes(x=0), lty=2) +
		ylab(xlab) +
		xlab(ylab) #switch because of the coord_flip() above
    return(p)
}

# Create some dummy data.
d <- data.frame(x = toupper(letters[1:10]),
                y = rnorm(10, .05, 0.1))
d <- transform(d, ylo = y-1/10, yhi=y+1/10)

forestplot(d)

On Wed, Oct 24, 2012 at 7:30 PM, Steve Ampah <steve...@gmail.com> wrote:

x<- c(rnorm(30),rnorm(30))
y<-rep(c("A","B","C"),20)

data<-data.frame(x,y)

ggplot(data,aes( x )+geom_histogram(binwidth=1)+facet_grid(y~.,margins=T)

> > I want a histogram of x across y so that with each A the total is 100% , that is if within A there are 4 blocks I expect percentages like 10%, 30% , 40%, 20%, and something similar for B and C.

You'll have to bin things outside of ggplot and then compute the percentages for each bin.

From: https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help/2008-January/151594.html
If you want the SAME bins as used by hist(), you can use:
hist(Vec, breaks = ..., plot = FALSE)$counts

Another alternative is to use cut() to bin a vector and return a factor,
upon which you can then use table() to get the counts. For example:

   table(cut(Vec, breaks = ...))

See ?hist and ?cut for more information.

HTH,
Marc Schwartz

No, not a bug, but rather a (very common!) misunderstanding of what xlim/ylim do. Basically, xlim/ylim throw away data, not scale axes; I suggest reading the examples in ?coord_cartesian.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

On Wed, Oct 24, 2012 at 2:13 PM, Wasteva <steve...@gmail.com> wrote:
>  Can someone help me to include corresponding percentages of histograms sit
> on the individual blocks. Please I don't mean percentages on the y-axis.

There are really two issues here: 1) getting percentages on the
y-axis, and 2) getting the labels on top of the bars.

For the first one:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=mpg, y=..count../sum(..count..))) +
   geom_histogram() +
   scale_y_continuous("Percent", labels=percent)

For the second one:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=mpg, y=..count.., label=..count..)) +
   geom_histogram() +
   geom_text(stat="bin")

putting it all together we get

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=mpg, y=..count../sum(..count..),
label=scales::percent(..count../sum(..count..)))) +
   geom_histogram() +
   geom_text(stat="bin") +
   scale_y_continuous("Percent", labels=percent)

Hope that helps!
Ista

  scale_color_manual(values = c("#000000", "#666666", "#CCCCCC")) +

  scale_linetype(guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = "black")))

Charlotte

messages.body_plain:
i am not sure if there is a r command to do it, but i manipulated the data and got what i want. i am posting the code here just in case someone else need it.

x <- matrix(c(45,53,35,66,49,60,1.9,7.9,9.3,1.4,5.7,2.6), nrow = 6, ncol = 2)
colnames(x) <- c("x1","x2")
y <- matrix(c(1.1,0.98,1,0.78,0.75,1.2,0.98,1.6,2.1,1.40,1.54,1.5,
               26.70,32.9,35.60,32.5,32.1,38.3,1,2.10,3.00,3.8,3.90,2.5),nrow=6,ncol=4)
colnames(y) <- c("y1","y2","y3","y4")
corr <- cor(x, y, use = "complete")
n <- nrow(corr)
m <- ncol(corr)
nx <- nrow(x)
mx <- ncol(x)
ny <- nrow(y)
my <- ncol(y)

##output p matrix

pmatrix <- matrix(NA, nrow = n, ncol = m)
for (i in 1:n){
  for (j in 1:m){
    pmatrix[i,j] = rcorr(x[,i], y[,j])$P[1,2]
  }
}

## set up variable names
rname <- rownames(corr)
cname <- colnames(corr)
options(digits=2)
new.data <- matrix(NA, nrow = n, ncol = 4)
new.x <- rep(rname, each = my)
new.y <- rep(cname, mx)
new.corr <- round(matrix(c(corr[,1],corr[,2],corr[,3],corr[,4])),2)
new.p <- round(matrix(c(pmatrix[,1],pmatrix[,2],pmatrix[,3],pmatrix[,4])),2)
new.data <- as.data.frame(cbind(new.x,new.y,new.corr,new.p))

# ggplot2 base layer
p <- ggplot(new.data)

# Bubble plots
p + geom_point(aes(x = new.x, y = new.y, size = new.corr, colour = new.p),shape=16, alpha=0.80)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Manuel:

It's a confidence band. Here's a toy example:

DF <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 0.4 + 0.6 * (1:10) + rnorm(10, sd = 0.5))
m <- lm(y ~ x, data = DF)

lmdata <- data.frame(DF, predict(m, interval = "confidence"))
ggplot(lmdata, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_line(aes(y = lwr), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(aes(y = upr), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm")

Dennis

Hi Manuel:

It's a confidence band. Here's a toy example:

DF <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 0.4 + 0.6 * (1:10) + rnorm(10, sd = 0.5))

m <- lm(y ~ x, data = DF)

lmdata <- data.frame(DF, predict(m, interval = "confidence"))

ggplot(lmdata, aes(x, y)) +

    geom_point() +

    geom_line(aes(y = lwr), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +

    geom_line(aes(y = upr), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +

    geom_smooth(method = "lm")

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am adding to lines of text to the last facet of a facet_grid plot and I get 4 warning messages saying that "NAs introduced by coercion".

The code for the plot is below and the plot that is produced looks fine. It is just the annoying warnings that do not appear if I remove the geom_text geoms. Any suggestions as to why I am getting these messages?

Cheers,

Chris

x.lev <- levels(Sources)
annot <- data.frame(Inf, -Inf, factor(x.lev[length(x.lev)], levels = x.lev))
names(annot) <- c("xDay",  "backtransformed.predictions", "Sources")
 windows()
  pred.plot <-  ggplot(data=backtransforms,
                         aes_string(x = x.var, y = "backtransformed.predictions")) +
                         scale_colour_manual(values=cbPalette) +
                         scale_shape_manual(values=symb) +
                         scale_x_continuous(x.title) +
                         scale_y_continuous(y.title) +
                         layer(geom = "line", colour = cbPalette[1]) +
                         layer(geom = "point", shape = symb[7])  +
                         facet_grid(~ Sources)
pred.plot <- pred.plot + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=lower.confidence.limit, ymax=upper.confidence.limit),
                                    alpha=0.2, fill="blue", show_guide=FALSE) + scale_fill_hue() +
                          geom_text(data = annot, label = "Error bars are",
                                    hjust=1, vjust=-1.3, size = 2) +
                          geom_text(data = annot, label = "confidence intervals",
                                    hjust=1, vjust=-0.3, size = 2)
pred.plot

messages.body_plain:
Hm, I think that's probably a bug. It seems to not be reversing the xend and yend values for annotate(). I've filed it here:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/706

In the meantime, you can create a separate data frame for the segment annotation, and use it with geom_segment:

segment <- data.frame(x=34.00, y=-0.3, xend = 34.5, yend = -0.1)

ggplot(C, aes(Salinity, dO18, color=Site)) +
  geom_point(size=3) +
  geom_segment(data=segment, aes(x=x, y=y, xend=xend, yend=yend),
               linetype=2, color="black") +
  scale_y_reverse()

-Winston

On 10/26/2012 10:12 AM, stan wrote:
> When use the example on p. 108 of the Wickam "ggplot2" text,

To make this reproducible for those that don't have the book at
hand/memorized:

plot <- qplot(brainwt, bodywt, data=msleep, log="xy")

> and inlcude the follwoing line:
>   plot  + aes(linetype=vore) + scale_linetype_manual(value=c(0,1,2,3,4))
>
> the output plots no lines.

I get an error:

Error in structure(list(call = match.call(), aesthetics = aesthetics,  :
   argument "values" is missing, with no default

The argument should be `values`, not `value`

Making that change:

plot  + aes(linetype=vore) + scale_linetype_manual(values=c(0,1,2,3,4))

does not have lines. But that has nothing to do with the manual
linetype. The issue is that qplot makes points by default. Points have
shape and colour, but not a linetype. You need to draw lines before you
see the effect of a linetype.

plot + geom_line() + aes(linetype=vore) +
scale_linetype_manual(values=c(1,2,3,4), na.value=0)

> I must be using the manual function incorrectly.
>
> Any suggestions?

--

Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: Re: Using stat_smooth with more than one explanatory variable
messages.subject_clean: Using stat_smooth with more than one explanatory variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi Manuel:

It appears that the method for computing confidence bands for GLMs in stat_smooth() follows this script:

(i)  find the predicted values on the linear predictor scale; call them LPhat;
(ii) compute LPhat +/- 1.96 * se.fit(LPhat)
(iii) apply the inverse link function on the lower and upper CIs.

What stat_smooth() does is to take 80 equally spaced x-values along its range, apply the above algorithm to those x's and then plot the result. We can see whether or not this hypothesis is correct on the kyphosis data. I'm using the version of the kyphosis data in the gam package, which supports the 1990 Hastie and Tibshirani book.

library(gam)
data(kyphosis)
km <- glm(as.numeric(Kyphosis) - 1 ~ Age, data = kyphosis)

# predict.glm() returns a list rather than a data frame
# so we need to do a little work to get the confidence bands
# The plot from your code indicates that at fixed x values,
# the intervals are not necessarily symmetric, which suggests
# some transformation of the limits is performed.

# Get the predictions on the linear predictor scale (default):
kmp <- predict(km, se.fit = TRUE)

# Compute intervals since no 'method =' argument exists in predict.glm():
kmpdf <- data.frame(Age = kyphosis$Age,
                   lwr = kmp$fit - 1.96 * kmp$se.fit,
                   upr = kmp$fit + 1.96 * kmp$se.fit)

The y-variable in the plot is the response, not the linear predictor. By definition, in logistic regression, under the canonical link function g() of a response probability p,
          g(p) = beta_0 + beta_1 * x1 + beta_2 * x2 + ... + beta_p * xp

The function g() in this case is the canonical logit link function, while the right hand side of the equation is the linear predictor. Life is simplest in this case, because we can then write
            p = g^{-1}(linear predictor).

The confidence bands for the probability of positive response p are obtained in stat_smooth() by applying the inverse link function g^{-1} to the upper and lower limits upr and lwr, respectively, in kmpdf:

The canonical link function for logistic regression is the logit function:
                   logit(p) = log(p/(1 - p))
The inverse link function is the logistic function
                   logis(x) = exp(x)/(1 + exp(x))
This is what will be applied to lwr and upr:
#----

logis <- function(x) exp(x)/(1 + exp(x))

library(plyr)
kmpdf <- mutate(kmpdf, llim = logis(lwr), ulim = logis(upr))

# Now do the plot:

qplot(Age, as.numeric(Kyphosis) - 1, data = kyphosis) +

    stat_smooth(method = "glm", family = "binomial") +
    geom_line(data = kmpdf, aes(x = Age, y = llim),
                        color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(data = kmpdf, aes(x = Age, y = ulim),
                        color = "red", linetype = "dashed")

#----
The limits should match.

By contrast, another approach would be to compute the predicted values on the response scale and use a Wald-based CI for p, which I think is what Thierry proposed:

kmp2 <- predict(km, type = "response", se.fit = TRUE)
kmpdf2 <- data.frame(Age = kyphosis$Age,
                lwr = kmp2$fit - 1.96 * kmp2$se.fit,
                upr = kmp2$fit + 1.96 * kmp2$se.fit)
last_plot() +
    geom_line(data = kmpdf2, aes(x = Age, y = lwr),
                       color = "black", linetype = "dotdash") +
    geom_line(data = kmpdf2, aes(x = Age, y = upr),
                       color = "black", linetype = "dotdash")

I'm not going to get into whether which one of these is "right"; in fact, there are other ways (e.g. likelihood-based intervals) one could use. But to answer the question, it appears that stat_smooth() renders intervals that are computed on the linear predictor scale which are then transformed according to the inverse link function. I haven't tried this out with Poisson regression or different link functions in logistic regression to verify that hypothesis - I'll leave that as an exercise.

Finally, note that se.fit on the linear predictor scale (in kmp) is not the same as se.fit on the response scale (in kmp2). This is because the response (under the canonical logit link function) is the inverse link of the linear predictor, so its standard error needs to take into account that transformation - this is where the "delta method" of computing the standard error of a transformed estimator comes into play indirectly. Computationally, the details are taken care of in the GLM fitting algorithm.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject_clean: Getting the lm equation
messages.body_plain:
For starters, by using method=loess isn't using lm()...

Secondly, here is some old code to pull out the coefficients and r^2, and then put them on a simple plot. If you want to do this over facets, it's more complicated, but entirely doable.

##Create linear model for y=mx + b and r^2

m <- lm(Smell ~ WIBI_5d, data = lm.data)

p <- ggplot(lm.data, aes(x = Smell, y = WIBI_5d)) + geom_smooth(method = "lm") + geom_point()

eq <- substitute(italic(y) == a + b %.% italic(x)*","~~italic(r)^2~"="~r2,
list(
a = format(coef(m)[1], digits = 4),
b = format(coef(m)[2], digits = 4),
r2 = format(summary(m)$r.squared, digits = 3)))

dftext <- data.frame(eq = as.character(as.expression(eq)))

p<-p + geom_text(aes(label = eq, x=3, y=2), data = dftext, parse = TRUE)

ggplot(iris, aes(Petal.Length, Petal.Width)) + geom_jitter(size = 4)

messages.subject: Re: Trouble with scale_shape_manual()
messages.subject_clean: Trouble with scale_shape_manual()
messages.body_plain:
On 10/29/2012 2:08 AM, Robert Latest wrote:
> Hello all,
>
> I'm trying to manually manipulate a shape scale using a "palette"
> function. The documentation says:
>
>      discrete_scale {ggplot2}
>
>      palette
>      a palette function that when called with a single integer argument
> (the number of levels in the scale) returns the values that they
> should take
>
> so I built a primitive function that IMO does just that: return a
> numeric vector (starting at 21, see definition of p.test below).
>
> When run the script below, I get an error message that fails to tell
> me anything: "Error in as.character(x$label) : cannot coerce type
> 'closure' to vector of type 'character'"
>
> What's going on here?
> Thanks, robert
>
> library(ggplot2)
>
> df <- data.frame(x=1:4, y=1:4, s=factor(1:4))
> plt <- ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, shape=s)) + geom_point()
>
> # print(plt) # works
>
> p.test <- function(n) { 21:(20+n) }
> print(plt + scale_shape_manual(palette=p.test)) # gives this error:
>
> # Error in as.character(x$label) :
> #  cannot coerce type 'closure' to vector of type 'character'

[As an aside, only part of this is directed at you, Robert; much of it
is meant for the developers, so don't worry if it gets obscure and
technical. I've summarized bits throughout and at the end.]

The manual scales do not have a palette argument. From the
scale_shape_manual page, ... is said to be able to take "common discrete
scale parameters: name, breaks, labels, na.value, limits and guide."
That is an inclusive list, not an example list. In particular, palette
is not a argument that (is meant to be) passed through to a discrete
scale. Now here is where it gets tricky.

By passing a palette, you do override the palette that the manual scale
internally creates from the values argument (which you don't provide).
Because of the argument matching based on named arguments and positional
matching, your passed palette becomes the one used and the internally
determined palette gets kicked to the next argument which happens to be
the name of the guide. (Which explains why when I was debugging, the
error was coming from a text grob.)  In particular note:

 > dput(scale_shape_manual(palette=p.test))
structure(list(call = discrete_scale(aesthetics = aesthetic,
     scale_name = "manual", palette = ..1, name = pal), aesthetics =
"shape",
     scale_name = "manual", palette = function (n)
     {
         21:(20 + n)
     }, range = <S4 object of class structure("DiscreteRange", package =
"scales")>,
     limits = NULL, na.value = NA, expand = structure(list(), class =
"waiver"),
     name = function (n)
     {
         if (n > length(values)) {
             stop("Insufficient values in manual scale. ", n,
                 " needed but only ", length(values), " provided.",
                 call. = FALSE)
         }
         values
     }, breaks = structure(list(), class = "waiver"), labels =
structure(list(), class = "waiver"),
     legend = NULL, drop = TRUE, guide = "legend"), .Names = c("call",
"aesthetics", "scale_name", "palette", "range", "limits", "na.value",
"expand", "name", "breaks", "labels", "legend", "drop", "guide"
), class = c("manual", "discrete", "scale"))

So, part 1, you should not give a palette argument to a scale_*_manual
function, but ggplot is not doing a good job of protecting its arguments
when you do.

The code you should have used is

plt + scale_shape_discrete(palette=p.test)

... except that doesn't work either do to a similar bug in a different
function. scale_shape_discrete also defines its own palette and passes
that along positionally and thus kicks some other function into the name
which gives the same (effective) error as it tries to write the name of
the legend which is a function instead of a string.

So, part 2, if you do specify it as you are supposed to, it still won't
work because of a bug.

Apparently, despite this palette functionality being there for awhile,
no one has actually attempted to use it before to realize it was broken.

So follow Brandon's advice and specify values instead. At least until
this functionality is working.

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University
