>> plt <- ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, shape=s)) + geom_point()
>>
>> # print(plt) # works
>>
>> p.test <- function(n) { 21:(20+n) }
>> print(plt + scale_shape_manual(palette=p.test)) # gives this error:
>>
>> # Error in as.character(x$label) :
>> #  cannot coerce type 'closure' to vector of type 'character'
>
> [As an aside, only part of this is directed at you, Robert; much of it
> is meant for the developers, so don't worry if it gets obscure and
> technical. I've summarized bits throughout and at the end.]
>
> The manual scales do not have a palette argument. From the
> scale_shape_manual page, ... is said to be able to take "common discrete
> scale parameters: name, breaks, labels, na.value, limits and guide."
> That is an inclusive list, not an example list. In particular, palette
> is not a argument that (is meant to be) passed through to a discrete
> scale. Now here is where it gets tricky.
>
> By passing a palette, you do override the palette that the manual scale
> internally creates from the values argument (which you don't provide).
> Because of the argument matching based on named arguments and positional
> matching, your passed palette becomes the one used and the internally
> determined palette gets kicked to the next argument which happens to be
> the name of the guide. (Which explains why when I was debugging, the
> error was coming from a text grob.)  In particular note:
>
>  > dput(scale_shape_manual(palette=p.test))
> structure(list(call = discrete_scale(aesthetics = aesthetic,
>      scale_name = "manual", palette = ..1, name = pal), aesthetics =
> "shape",
>      scale_name = "manual", palette = function (n)
>      {
>          21:(20 + n)
>      }, range = <S4 object of class structure("DiscreteRange", package =
> "scales")>,
>      limits = NULL, na.value = NA, expand = structure(list(), class =
> "waiver"),
>      name = function (n)
>      {
>          if (n > length(values)) {
>              stop("Insufficient values in manual scale. ", n,
>                  " needed but only ", length(values), " provided.",
>                  call. = FALSE)
>          }
>          values
>      }, breaks = structure(list(), class = "waiver"), labels =
> structure(list(), class = "waiver"),
>      legend = NULL, drop = TRUE, guide = "legend"), .Names = c("call",
> "aesthetics", "scale_name", "palette", "range", "limits", "na.value",
> "expand", "name", "breaks", "labels", "legend", "drop", "guide"
> ), class = c("manual", "discrete", "scale"))
>
> So, part 1, you should not give a palette argument to a scale_*_manual
> function, but ggplot is not doing a good job of protecting its arguments
> when you do.
>
> The code you should have used is
>
> plt + scale_shape_discrete(palette=p.test)
>
> ... except that doesn't work either do to a similar bug in a different
> function. scale_shape_discrete also defines its own palette and passes
> that along positionally and thus kicks some other function into the name
> which gives the same (effective) error as it tries to write the name of
> the legend which is a function instead of a string.
>
> So, part 2, if you do specify it as you are supposed to, it still won't
> work because of a bug.
>
> Apparently, despite this palette functionality being there for awhile,
> no one has actually attempted to use it before to realize it was broken.

Actually, looking at the documentation for scale_shape, it is not stated
that it can take a palette argument either. Apparently you can only
specify palette if you create your own scale.

plt + discrete_scale("shape", "shape", palette=p.test)

> So follow Brandon's advice and specify values instead. At least until
> this functionality is working.
>

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: Re: Constant scale values not inherited
messages.subject_clean: Constant scale values not inherited
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Oct 29, 2012 at 9:56 AM, ggrothendieck <ggroth...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> On Friday, June 1, 2012 8:12:24 AM UTC-4, Karl Ove Hufthammer wrote:
>>
>> Dear list members,
>>
>> Please see the following examples:
>>
>>   qplot(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, data=iris, colour=Species, size=I(4)) +
>> geom_jitter()
>>   qplot(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, data=iris, colour=Species, pch=I(2)) +
>> geom_jitter()
>>
>> It looks like only the non-jittered points ‘inherit’ the size and shape
>> values. It looks like a bug to me, but perhaps the ‘contant’ values are
>> only *supposed* to apply to points? For example, using geom_path(),
>>
>>   qplot(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, data=iris, colour=Species, size=I(4)) +
>> geom_path()
>>
>> only the points change size, not the lines. Note that using
>> geom="jitter" or geom="path" *inside* qplot, things work as expected.
>>
>> So, is this non-inheritance of constant/literal values a feature or a
>> bug?
>>
>
> I am dredging this up from a few months ago since I have come across this
> too and it seems a true problem or at least unexpected and not just a matter
> of using ggplot vs. qplot as suggested by some of the responders.  In the
> jitter code example that was used in this thread the layer does not inherit
> size=4 so
>
> ggplot(iris, aes(Petal.Length, Petal.Width), size = 4) + geom_jitter()
>
> is not identical to:
>
> ggplot(iris, aes(Petal.Length, Petal.Width)) + geom_jitter(size = 4)
>
> I would have expected both to give the same answer based on the idea that
> the layers inherit defaults from the ggplot() args.

Yes, only mapped aesthetics (those inside of mapping=aes()) are
inherited. If you try to _set_ an aesthetic in ggplot(), it has no
effect. That's the way it is, although I guess it's debatable whether
that's the way it should be.

-Winston

Hi Thiago,

Glad it was useful. Note that geom_histogram is just an alias for
stat_bin plus geom_bar, basically; I believe that you can do something
like this for a relative histogram:

p <- ggplot( dump, aes( as.factor( Classes ), value ) )
p + stat_bin(aes(y=..density..*binwidth), position="dodge", binwidth=binwidth)

...where 'binwidth' is whatever you want. I haven't tested
this--sorry, can't right now--but think it will do what you want.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: overlaying histograms legend?
messages.subject_clean: overlaying histograms legend?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This is an example of 'creating a factor on the fly', illustrated in the ggplot2 book.

ggplot(dat,aes(x=date)) +
    geom_histogram(data=subset(dat,type == 'original'), aes(fill = "Original"),
                             alpha = 0.5, binwidth =  1) +
    geom_histogram(data=subset(dat,type == 'subsample'), aes(fill = "Subsample"),
                             alpha = 0.8, binwidth = 1) +
    labs(x = "Month", y = "Count", fill = "Data type") +
    ggtitle("Sampling Distributions\n")  +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("red", "blue"))

The last line is to specify the colors you defined in your code.

Dennis

> effect. That's the way it is, although I guess it's debatable whether
> that's the way it should be.
>
> -Winston

The argument in favor of having all ggplot() arguments be inherited by the layers is simplicity.

One could then have a more compact description of how it works.  Namely ggplot() could inherit globals and then layers could inherit from ggplot like this (where we have termed settings that are set via update_geom_defaults as globals):

   globals <- ggplot() <- layers.

Right now layers inherit some things from globals set via update_geom_defaults() and some things from ggplot() so it looks like this (at least conceptually - this may not be how it works internally):

   globals <- layers
   ggplot() <- layers

which is harder to understand since one would need to remember which is inherited from which.

Ideally one could just say that layers inherit from ggplot() which inherits from the global defaults.

I have a problem using the grid.arrange function in the gridExtra package to put multiple plots in one window. In attach you can find the dput output with the two datasets. Below you can find the code I used to create the plots.

plot.J.SVI<-ggplot(div.env,aes(SVI,J))+geom_point()+geom_smooth(se=F,method="lm",colour="black")+labs(y="J'",x="SVI")+opts(panel.grid.major=theme_blank(),panel.grid.minor=theme_blank())

messages.body_plain:
Try:
x1 <- data.frame(x=1:10,y=(1:10)^2)
ggplot(x1, aes(x,y) ) + labs(x="X values", y = "Y values", title = expression(paste("Some text: ",x^2, "some more text: ",y[3]))) + geom_point()
